newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia passes budget with little peace dividend.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia passes budget with little peace dividend.

text.p: Cambodia's national assembly has passed a 1.5 trillion riel ($556 million) spending package for 1997 with heavy expenditures on defence, sparking a national debate on what has become of a promised peace dividend.

The spending bill, adopted on Monday, earmarks about $150 million for defence spending, or roughly one quarter of the budget, for 1997 -- a year which many believe will see the end of the country's waning civil war.

The Khmer Rouge, which has been fighting the coalition government formed after U.N.-sponsored elections in 1993, has crumbled in the wake of massive defections, and defence officials say there will be no need to launch the annual dry season offensive against the Maoist guerrillas, whose numbers are believed to have dwindled to less than 2,000.
For many, that means spending should be diverted from defence.
"I am very sad. I condemn this budget," said opposition leader Sam Rainsy, who heads the unrecognised Khmer Nation Party.

"There are a lot of powerful interests who collect a lot of money for their own benefit under the pretext of war, and now it is under the pretext of making peace," he said in apparent reference to the military.
"We continue to spend the national budget on warlords and for political parties, and not for the development and reconstruction of the country," he noted.
But defence officials counter that peace with the Khmer Rouge, which led the brutal 1975-1979 "killing fields" regime, comes at a cost.
"There are 10,000 Khmer Rouge who defected, and we have to clothe them, feed them and take care of them," said Ek Sereywath, secretary of state for the defence ministry.
Chum Sambath, spokesman for defence, noted the defence budget is slightly lower than last year, reflecting lowered spending on weapons.
As Cambodia absorbs the financial burden of incorporating its former enemies into its own armed forces, analysts say it also faces rising social demands and economic strains.
The nation's per capita gross domestic product is under $300, and a tiny tax base and heavy dependence on foreign aid undermine economic growth, economic analysts noted.
They applauded increased spending on agriculture, health, and education, but questioned whether the country can also sufficiently increase its revenue.
The National Assembly is debating the tax law portion of the budget, but did not pass it on Tuesday. ($1 = 2,700 riel)
